title: Set a bill-of-materials cost target and protect it
summary: In hardware, the parts list sets most of the cost of every unit you sell. Agree a target cost per unit early and check every design change against it.

beginner: Learn what a bill of materials (BOM) is: every part, material and sub-assembly in one unit.
Work out the price customers will pay and the margin the business needs.
Turn that into a target cost per unit, and write it into the product brief.
Ask engineering for a first costed BOM and compare it with the target.
Agree a rule: any change that adds cost needs your sign-off.
intermediate: Set a target unit cost from price, margin and expected volume.
Review the costed BOM with engineering and purchasing at each build.
Track the gap to target and agree trade-offs before they reach the design.
experienced: Set cost targets across a product line, including packaging, freight and returns.
Plan cost-down steps for later production runs.
Make unit cost a standing measure in portfolio reviews.

canDelegateTo.task: Produce and maintain the costed BOM

toolExamples.sharepoint-word: Keep the costed BOM in a shared spreadsheet with a change log.
toolExamples.google-docs: Track the target and current unit cost on the first tab of the BOM sheet.

definitionOfDone: Target unit cost agreed and written down
First costed BOM compared with the target
Rule for approving cost increases agreed
pitfalls: Setting the target after the design is fixed
Letting small additions pile up unchecked

leaderView.good: Each product has a target cost per unit, agreed early and protected through design changes.
ask: What's our target cost per unit, and where are we against it?
Which design changes have added cost?
signs: Cost is only checked when quotes arrive.
Features are added without a cost check.
